chapters.title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Geopolitics for Markets

lessons.title: Case Study: How the Nifty and Gold Reacted in the First Week of the Russia-Ukraine War

body.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine gives you a clean, single-event test of everything covered in this chapter: the four channels, the power-resources-alliances framework, and the VIX-and-gold fear signals, all playing out in the Indian market within the same fortnight.

children.text: Every framework in this chapter so far has been explained in the abstract. This case study puts them to work on one real event: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and the roughly two weeks of Indian market reaction that followed. Treat this lesson as a template. The specific numbers belong to February and March 2022, but the sequence, escalation, shock, peak fear, and recovery, repeats across most geopolitical events you will study in this course.

events.title: Recognition of Donetsk and Luhansk
events.description: Russia formally recognised the two breakaway regions of eastern Ukraine as independent and moved troops in, widely seen as the clearest pre-invasion signal yet. Indian markets slipped moderately, pricing rising but not yet certain risk.

events.title: Full invasion begins
events.description: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Nifty and Sensex fell sharply the same day, widely reported at around 4.5 to 4.8 percent, among the sharpest single-day falls since the COVID-19 crash nearly two years earlier. Brent crude briefly crossed $100 a barrel intraday for the first time since 2014.

events.title: Oil fear peaks
events.description: As sanctions tightened and fears grew over Russian energy supply, Brent crude spiked further, briefly trading close to its highest levels since 2008. India VIX stayed elevated through this window, and the Nifty made its lowest point of the episode around this period, roughly two weeks after the invasion headline itself, not on day one.

events.title: Recovery, despite the war continuing
events.description: The Nifty recovered a large part of its initial losses through March even though the war itself was far from over. This is the pattern worth remembering: markets react hardest to new, unpriced information, not to the ongoing existence of a conflict once its immediate shock has been absorbed.

body.caption: Approximate Market Snapshot Around the Invasion

cells: Spiked into the high 20s to low 30s
Made its lowest point of the episode
Spiked close to its highest level since 2008
Recovered a large part of the initial fall
Eased back toward its calmer range
Pulled back from its peak, though still elevated

body.text: Notice that the Nifty's actual low point came roughly two weeks after the invasion, not on the invasion day itself. The initial headline was priced almost instantly, but the market kept reacting as long as new information, chiefly around oil supply and sanctions, kept arriving. Peak fear and the initial headline are not always the same moment.

body.caption: The Four Channels, As Seen in This Event

cells: Brent crude's spike above $100, then toward its highest level since 2008, directly raised India's import bill and fed into domestic fuel and inflation worries
The rupee weakened alongside the broader risk-off move, compounding the effective cost of imported crude, while gold in INR terms benefited from both global safe-haven buying and the weaker rupee

Foreign institutional investors were net sellers of Indian equities through this window, a pattern consistent with a broad, global flight from risk assets rather than anything specific to Indian company fundamentals

India's direct trade with Russia and Ukraine was comparatively small, so this channel mattered far less here than energy, currency, and capital flows did, an important contrast with events later in this course

children.text: Which Sectors Actually Moved, and Why

cells: All are heavy users of crude-linked inputs, aviation turbine fuel, raw materials for paint, and rubber and crude derivatives for tyres, so a crude spike raises costs directly
The most FII-heavy part of the Nifty, so a broad risk-off move and foreign selling hit this segment hard regardless of individual bank fundamentals

Russia is a significant global producer of metals like nickel, palladium, and aluminium, so fears of supply disruption pushed some global metal prices, and Indian metal stocks tracking them, higher even as the broader market fell
Limited direct business exposure to Russia or Ukraine, but still dragged down by the broader global risk-off move and its correlation with weaker US technology stocks

body.title: Which Channel Mattered Least Here?
body.question: Based on this case study, which of the four channels from the earlier lesson mattered comparatively LEAST in explaining India's market reaction to the Russia-Ukraine invasion?
body.explanation: India's direct trade exposure to Russia and Ukraine was comparatively small, so the trade and supply chains channel mattered far less here than energy, currency, and capital flows did. This is a useful contrast to keep in mind, since the same event can hit different channels with very different force depending on the countries involved.

body.title: Explaining the Delayed Bottom
body.scenario: A colleague argues that since the Nifty's steepest single-day fall came on the invasion day itself, 24 February 2022, that must also have been the market's low point for the episode. You know this is not quite right, the actual low came roughly two weeks later.
body.prompt: Explain to your colleague, in your own words, why the market's lowest point did not necessarily coincide with its sharpest single-day fall.
body.modelAnswer: The sharpest single-day fall reflects the shock of the initial, unexpected headline being priced in all at once. The eventual low point, however, depends on how the situation continues to unfold, in this case, further sanctions and a spike in oil prices toward early March kept adding new negative information even after the initial shock had been absorbed. Markets fall further when genuinely new bad news keeps arriving, not just because the initial event remains ongoing. Once no further negative surprises arrived and existing fears were fully priced in, the market began to recover, even though the war itself was continuing.

points: The Russia-Ukraine invasion offers a clean template for this chapter's frameworks: an initial sharp shock on the headline itself, followed by continued reaction to new information, and eventual recovery

The Nifty's sharpest single-day fall, around 4.5 to 4.8 percent on 24 February 2022, did not coincide with its actual low point for the episode, which came roughly two weeks later as oil prices kept climbing

Energy, currency, and capital flows were the dominant channels in this event; trade and supply chains mattered comparatively little, since India's direct trade exposure to Russia and Ukraine was small

Sector impact was uneven: crude-sensitive sectors like aviation, paints, and tyres were hit hardest, FII-heavy financials sold off on capital flows alone, while some metal stocks actually gained on global supply-disruption fears
Markets recovering while a conflict is still ongoing is a recurring pattern, not an anomaly. Prices react to new, unpriced information, not to the continued existence of a known situation
